SCHEDULE
Kandla Port Trust (Authorisation of Pilots) Regulations, 2013
In exercise of the powers conferred by Section 28 of the Major Port
Trusts Act, 1963 (38 of 1963) and in supersession of the Kandla Port
(Authorisation of Pilots) Regulations 1964, the Board of Trustees of the Port
of Kandla, hereby makes the following regulations, namely-
PART - I
1. Short title and commencement - (1) These Regulations may be called
the Kandla Port Trust (Authorization of Pilots) Regulations, 2013
(2) These Regulations shall come into force from the date of publication
in the official Gazette.
2. Definitions. - In these regulations, unless the context otherwise requires:-
(a) “Board”, “Chairman” and “Deputy Chairman” shall have the same
meaning as in the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963 (38 of 1963);
(b) “Control Station” Means the station through which the direction
of management of pilotage is vested;
(c) “Deputy Conservator” means the Officer in whom the direction
and the management of Pilotage are vested;
(d) “Harbour Master” means the Officer appointed to perform such
duties as may, from time to time, be assigned to him by the Deputy
Conservator:
(e) “Limits of Compulsory Pilotage Waters” mean the limits defined
under sub-section [2] of Section 4 of the Indian Parts Act. 1908
(15 of 1908);
36

37
(f) “Outer Tuna Buoy” means the name of the fairway buoy at the
entry point of incoming Vessels. Pilotage is compulsory and the
Pilots board the incoming vessels and disembark from outgoing
vessels at pilotage point near Outer Tuna Buoy;
(g) “Master” or “Master of the Vessel” includes any officer (except a
Pilot or Harbour Master) having overall command or charge of the
vessel and is required to keep all equipment required towards the
safety of the vessel, in readiness, which includes anchoring and
steering of the vessel;
(h) “Pilot” means an Officer licensed under these regulations to perform
pilotage duty of guiding the ships to and fro the Port in all advisory
capacity and works directly under Harbour Master and Deputy
Conservator;
(i) “Pilot Licence” means Licence issued to a person to carry out
pilotage of vessels within the port limits of the Port.
(j) “Port” means the Port of Kandla.
PART - II
Licensing - Qualifications and Conditions
3. Qualifications of candidates.-
(1) A candidate for Pilot Licence shall:-
(a) be an Indian national;
(b) produce certificates of good character and sobriety;
(c) be in possession of a :-
(i) Certificate of Competency as Master (Foreign Going)
granted by the Government of India or its equivalent
and have preferably experience of six months as First
Mate on a foreign going ship; OR

38
(ii) Certificate as Dredge Master issued by the Directorate
General of Shipping and have preferably experience
of two years as a Dredge Master; OR
(iii) have successfully completed training as Pilot under
the ln-house Training of Pilots at the Port, as may be
decided by the Board from time to time in consultation
with the Director General of Shipping
(d) obtain a certificate of physical fitness from such medical
authority
(e) unless the Chairman otherwise determines serve a period of
probationary training of not less than six months and
successfully pass the prescribed examination.
Provided that the period of probationary training may be extended beyond
six months for sufficient and valid reasons such as:-
(i) candidate is unable to complete required phases of training due to
his own illness, or has to proceed on leave for sufficient and valid
reasons or due to any national emergency etc.;
(ii) in the interest of the Port or Government of India, the candidate is
required to be allotted some other duties (with prior agreement)
such as Dredging Master, Berthing Master, etc., and is thus unable
to complete his training requirement;
(iii) candidate for valid reasons is unable to pass his examination
during the stipulated period of twelve months and in the view of
the Chairman, needs to be given a fair chance to pass the
examination;
(iv) in case of candidates belonging to SC/ST, special extra training or
guidance is deemed necessary;

39
Provided further that the period of probationary training may be curtailed
under the following circumstances:
(i) if the candidate has been a Pilot in the said Port Trust and has
rejoined subsequently;
(ii) if in future modern technology such as a simulator is used for
training
(2) Position in Station, description and flags and signal of Identification
of Pilots launch or boat.–
(1) The Pilot will board incoming vessels and disembark from outgoing
Vessels by Pilot launch at Outer Tuna Buoy.
(2) The launch or boat will have the word ‘PILOT’ amidships on each
side
(3) The Pilot launch when on station, shall -
(a) during the day time, exhibit a red and white flag, the upper
horizontal half of which shall be white and the lower horizontal
will be red; and
(b) during night, exhibit lights in accordance with the rules or
law for the time being in force.
(3) The Pilot Station and Shore Station.  - The Harbour Master through
Signal Station shall monitor the boarding and disembarking of Pilots and
shall exercise control over them.
(4) Harbour Master’s control over the Pilot. - The Harbour Master shall
have control over Pilots in pilotage charge of vessels while entering or
leaving the Port or mooring or berthing or unberthing at any anchorage
or berth in the Port. The Pilots shall not leave the headquarter without
prior permission from the Harbour Master or an Officer acting on his
behalf. While seeking permission to leave the headquarters the Pilot shall

40
give the address and the telephone number on which he can be contacted,
if required.
4. Pilot Licence. - (1) All Pilots shall hold Pilot Licence to perform the
duties of a Pilot for the Port of Kandla. This Licence for restricted pilotage or
full pilotage, subject to the sanction of the Central Government, shall be issued
under the signature of Chairman and sealed with the common seal of the Board
and revocable by the Chairman.
(2) A Pilot severing his connection from the Port shall forthwith
surrender his Pilot Licence to the Deputy Conservator.
(3) The Pilot Licence may be revoked by the Chairman in
circumstances such as:
(a) proven misconduct and/or misconduct under the conduct
and discipline rules;
(b) professional misconduct; (means wilful default or departure
from the Regulations concerning the pilotage in force from
time to time);
(c) shipping casualties (accidents) where professional
competence is questioned or negligence proved after enquiry
into the accident;
(d) where formal court of enquiry instituted into marine casualty
holds Pilots responsible for an accident;
(e) on cessation from service if the licence is not surrendered
as required under regulation (2) above; and
(f) on being medically found unsuitable for Pilotage jobs.
(4) A Pilot shall retain Licence on subsequent promotions in the Pilotage
services upto the post of Deputy Conservator and continue to pilot
vessels as per the requirement.

41
5. Conditions for joining the Pilot Service in Port.  - A person shall not
be appointed as a Pilot until and unless he satisfies the Chairman that he fulfils
the following conditions, namely:-
(a) The conditions of eligibility laid down in regulation 14(b) and 14(c)
of the Kandla Port Employees (Recruitment, Seniority and
Promotion) Regulations 1964;
(b) On the date of appointment as 3 Probationary Pilot he is of an age
not below 25 years but not exceeding 35 years unless otherwise
relaxed by the Chairman; and
(c) That he possesses the qualifications specified under Regulation 3.
PART - III
TRAINING  AND  EXAMINATION
6. Training. - (1) During the period of training, probationary pilot will
be instructed in duties of a Pilot, the lights, the landmarks, buoyage, etc. of the
Harbour, the handling of ships within the pilotage waters of the Port, berthing
or unberthing of vessels within the dock basins, handling the port
trust owned suction dredger and operating her dredging equipments, etc.
(a) On completion of the training, the probationary pilot may, subject
to the approval of Deputy Conservator, apply to be examined as to
his qualifications to pilot ships;
Provided that the period of Training be extended beyond three
months but not more than six months for sufficient and valid
reasons such as :-
(i) candidate is unable to complete required phases of training
due to his own illness, or has to proceed on leave for sufficient
and valid reasons or due to any national emergency, etc.;
(ii) candidate for valid reasons is unable to pass his examination

42
during the stipulated period and in the view of Chairman
needs to be given a fair chance to pass examination;
Provided further that the training during the period of probation may be
curtailed under the following circumstances:
(i) If the Pilot on probation has been a Pilot in Kandla Port
Trust or any other Major Port in the country and has rejoined
Kandla Port Trust subsequently;
(ii) if in future modern technology such as a simulator is used
for training.
(b) A candidate for a Restricted Pilotage Licence shall comply with
the requirements under (a) and unless the board determines, serve
a period of training of not less than one month or till such time he
attends a minimum of thirty Acts of Pilotage involving crossing
the channel whichever is later.
(c) On completion of the training, the probationary Pilot may, if
recommended by the Harbour Master and subject to the approval
of Deputy Conservator, apply to be examined for grant of restricted
pilotage licence.
(2) No fee for Pilot licencs is recovered as the Probationary Pilot is an
employee of the Port Trust and whenever the Pilot leaves the job from the Port
Trust the licence so issued to him is surrendered.
(3) The candidate selected for appointment, as a Pilot shall execute the Bond
to serve Kandla Port for a minimum period of five years on completion of
Probationary period of two years as per prescribed format at Appendix-A
attached to these Regulations. The indemnity amount should be equal to the
cost of training plus the amount being paid to the probationary Pilot as salary
or stipend.

43
7. Subjects of Examination. - The examination shall include the following
subjects, namely;
¾ regulations and rules framed for navigating in the Harbour and
approaches to the dock and piers;
¾ course and distance between any two places;
¾ rise and set of tides:
¾ depth and character of soundings;
¾ anchorages, rocks, shoals and other dangers, landmarks, buoys,
beacons and lights within the Port;
¾ management of ship and steamers, how to bring them to anchor
and to keep them clear of their anchors in a tideway:
¾ to moor and unmoor and get underway;
¾ to handle a vessel under all conditions; and
¾ such other subjects as may be determined by the Examination
Committee.
8. Examination Committee. – The examination of the Probationary Pilot
shall be conducted by an Examination Committee composed of as follows:
(i) The Deputy Conservator – Chairman
(ii) The Harbour Master – Member
(iii) A Master of a Foreign Going Ship – Member
On completion of prescribed training, the probationary Pilot may apply
to be examined for grant of restricted pilotage licence to the Deputy Conservator,
subject to recommendation by at least two senior Pilots and Harbour Master
regarding capability of the probationary Pilot to pilot vessels.

44
9. Failure to pass Examination. - (1) In the event of a probationary Pilot
failing to pass the specified examination within twelve months of his
appointment, he will be liable to be discharged.
(2) In the event of a probationary Pilot after completion of his training period
fails the examination, he will be given an extension of Training period and be
permitted to appear in the examination a second time. In case his
performance is not found satisfactory in the second examination also, his,
services as probationary Pilot will be terminated,
10. Issue of Licence. - (1) On successful completion of the examination,
the Pilot shall be issued the Pilot Licence under Regulation 4 above.
(2) The fee for a Pilot’s Licence, and for renewal thereof in case, of mutilation
or loss, shall be prescribed by the Board from time to time,
11. Classification of Pilots. - (1) A Pilot on being licensed will be permitted
to pilot V essels as follows:-
(a) during the first six months, attached to the berthing service and
perform berthing or unberthing of vessels (except dangerous
petroleum tankers, men-of-war and ships loaded with explosives)
not exceeding 11000 tonnes gross register during day light hours
only;
(b) during the next six months, vessels (except dangerous petroleum
tankers, men-of-war and ships loaded with explosives) not
exceeding 16000 tonnes gross register during day light hours only;
(c) during the next six months vessels (except dangerous petroleum
tankers, men-of-war and ships loaded with explosives) of 12000
tonnes gross register during hours of darkness;
(d) during the next six months, after passing a departmental examination
conducted by the Deputy Conservator and Harbour Master, vessels
of unrestricted tonnage, type and class during day light hours and

45
vessels upto 16000 tonnes gross register of any type or class during
hours of darkness.
(e) Thereafter, on completion of six months, full tonnage or open
tonnage i.e. all vessels without restriction during day and night
Note:-
(i) Transfer of Pilot from one class to the next higher class will be on
the recommendation of the Harbour Master and subject to the
approval of the Deputy Conservator,
(ii) The period of three months or six months as specified above shall
be extended by the period of leave, if any, availed by the Pilot.
Explanation. For the purpose of above rules, the “hour of darkness”
means half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise.
PART - IV
SHORE  STATION - MONITORING  AND  CONTROL
12. Duties of Pilots. - The duties of a Pilot shall include -
(a) Piloting of V essels in and out of the harbour, berthing, unberthing
and shifting of vessels;
(b) Take command of dredgers as and when necessary and Port crafts
or tugs when proceeding beyond Port limits and also in case of
contingencies like strike, etc. by the workers, on the instructions
of Deputy Conservator;
(c) To attend and monitor the pull back operations during pilotage at
Single Buoy Mooring (SBM) throughout the vessel’s stay.
13. Dock Masters to do duties at Shore Station.  - The Dock Masters at
various shore stations shall perform their duties, in rotation for such periods as
may from time to time be ordered by the Deputy Conservator. The Dock

46
Master at the control station shall perform such duties, including control of the
Vessel Traffic Service Station, as may be specified by the Deputy Conservator.
14. The Pilot Station and the Shore Station. - The Harbour Master at the
Control Station shall monitor the boarding and disembarking of Master Pilots
or Pilots and shall exercise control over them.
15. Operational Control of Pilots. -  The Harbour Master Shall have the
control over Master Pilots and Pilots in pilotage charges of vessels while entering
or leaving the port, mooring or unmooring and berthing or un-berthing at any
anchorage, berth, dock within the port.
16. Boarding inward bound - vessels, etc. -  The Harbour Master at the
Control Station shall ensure that the Master Pilot or Pilot on turn for boarding
inwards are duly boarded upon inbound vessels requiring Pilots. Also ensure
that Master Pilot or Pilot are disembarked from outbound vessels.
17. Power to direct Pilots to take charge of a Vessel of higher tonnage
in certain circumstances. - The Deputy Conservator or Harbour Master may,
if necessary direct a Pilot to pilot a vessel exceeding in tonnage the Vessels
which he is qualified for under regulation 12 to Pilot. In every/such case, the
Deputy
 Conservator or Harbour Master shall forthwith send a report in writing
to the Chairman stating the reasons which in his opinion necessitated such
action
18. Harbour Master to Regulate Attendance of Pilots on Vessels. - Pilots
on shore duty shall be detailed under the supervision of the Harbour Master to
vessels requiring their services and a list showing the rotation in which Pilots,
having regard to their respective classes, are to be allotted to such vessels shall
be drawn up and kept in the office of the Deputy Conservator or Harbour
Master. The allocation of Pilots’ for individual movements in accordance with
the list drawn up in the Deputy Conservator’s office and any adjustments
necessitated by changes or cancellations of allocations of Pilots shall be attended
to by the signal station.

47
PART - V
DUTIES OF PILOTS
19. Pilots to obey the order of the Authority. -  A Pilot shall obey and
execute all orders and regulations given or issued by the Chairman, the Deputy
Chairman, the Deputy Conservator and or the Harbour Master. He shall also
obey all orders given by Deputy Conservator or Harbour Master relating to
berthing, unberthing, shifting and towing of vessels under his charge.
20. Pilots Behaviour. - (1) A Pilot shall at all times exercise strict sobriety.
He shall be the incharge of the vessel throughout the time and use his utmost
care and diligence for her safety and the safety of other vessels and property.
He shall not lay by the vessel aground without a written order from the owner
or Officer in command.
(2) A Pilot is an employee of the Board and governed by the Kandla Port
Employees (Recruitment, Seniority and Promotion) Regulations for all
his service matters and, therefore, in the event of any misconduct or
misbehaviour while in service liable to disciplinary proceedings under
Kandla Port Employees (Classification, Control and Appeal) Regulations
as amended from time to time.
21. Pilots to obtain certificate of service performed by them. -  A Pilot
shall on boarding the vessel handover the arrival or departure report to the
Master who shall enter therein all the required particulars over his signature.
The arrival report shall be duly filled in and returned to the Pilot before the
vessel reaches middle ground the departure report before reaching Outer Tuna
Buoy. Transporting and anchoring certificates shall be filled by the pilot and
presented to the Master for signature when the duties of Pilot are completed.
22. Pilots to go on board vessels in good time. -  A pilot about to take
charge of a vessel which is outward bound, or which is about to be moved
from the berth in which she is lying, shall go on board and report himself to the

48
officer in command at the time appointed, i.e. in sufficient time for her to be
moved out to sea or to her destination.
23. Pilots to see that vessel and her equipment are in order. -  A pilot
before taking charge of an inward or outward bound vessel or shifting of
vessel shall enquire from the Master of the Vessel whether the steering gear is
connected and in proper working order and direct that both the anchors be
ready for letting go.
24. Pilot to acquaint with the movement of vessels. -  All Pilots prior to
boarding the vessel, acquaint themselves with the movement of vessels in the
harbour and the Pilot on board in each of them.
25. Commencement of Pilot’s outward duties. -  The duties of a Pilot in
regard to outward bound vessel shall commence on boarding the vessels at
any wharf, pier, jetty or anchorage.
26. Termination of Pilot’s outward duties. - The duties of a Pilot in regard
to an outward bound vessel shall cease when he has piloted the vessel upto the
limits of the compulsory pilotage waters (Outer Tuna Buoy);
27. Commencement of Pilot’s Inward duties. -  The duties of a Pilot in
regard to an inward bound vessel shall commence when he boards the vessel
at the pilot station within the compulsory pilotage limits of the Port (Outer
Tuna Buoy).
28. Termination of Pilot’s inward duties. - The duties of a Pilot in regard
to any inward bound vessel shall cease at any wharf, pier, berth or jetty or
anchorage when the vessel is safely moored, berthed and secured or anchored
However, in case of Single Buoy Mooring (SBM) operation, the Pilot will stay
on board to monitor the pull back operation throughout the vessel’s stay.
29. Moving of Vessel. -  No Pilot shall move or direct the moving of any
vessel within the Port from one position to another unless the following
conditions are fulfilled –

49
(i) if the vessel is underway, the Master shall be on board;
(ii) if the Master leaves the vessel before the movement is completed,
the Pilot shall direct the vessel to be anchored in such safe position
as may be most easily reached by the vessel and shall not give
directions to proceed with the moving until the return of the Master
to the vessel :-
(iii) throughout the moving the number of officers and crew on board
and available for duty shall be sufficient to perform any duty which
may be required, and if the Pilot on board considers that the number
is not sufficient, he shall call the Master’s attention to the Port
rules and refuse to proceed with the moving unless the Master
first signs a declaration under his own hand expressly assuming
entire responsibility.
Explanation: In this Regulation, the expression “Master” shall include
the first or other officer duly authorized to act for the Master in the event of
the latter being incapacitated from performing the duties of his office.
30. Pilots to report on landing, - On landing, after piloting a vessel inward
and or transporting a vessel in the stream, or returning from the pilot vessel, a
Pilot shall report without delay to the signal station the time of his landing
ashore by entering his name on the roster kept for this purpose, for further
duty.
31. Pilots not to bring vessels into dock when the signal is against
him.- A Pilot shall not bring a vessel into dock or alongside a berth unless
cleared to do so by the shore station.
32. Pilots when on duty to carry with them their licence, etc. -  A
Pilot when on duty shall always have with him an official Tide Table for
the Port, a copy of the Port rules, pilotage regulations presen tly in force and
his licence.

50
33. Loss of Licence. - A pilot losing his licence shall forthwith give notice
thereof to the Deputy Conservator, stating the circumstances in which the
licence was lost, and the Deputy Conservator shall unless he is satisfied that
the loss has been caused by the Pilot’s misconduct, issue the Pilot a temporary
licence pending the grant of a duplicate licence by the Chairman.
34. Pilots to give information of any alterations in navigational marks,
etc. - A pilot who has observed any alteration in the depth of the channels, or
has noticed that any buoys, beacons or light vessels have been driven away,
broken down, damaged or shifted from position, or has become aware of any
circumstances likely to affect the safety of navigation shall forthwith send a
detailed report thereof in writing to the Deputy Conservator
35. Pilots to report casualties. -  A Pilot, whenever, any accident has
happened to or been caused by a vessel while in his charge, shall as soon as
possible and not later than twenty four hours of the accident, report the facts
in writing in the form prescribed for the purpose as per Appendix-B, to the
Deputy Conservator.
36. Pilots to ascertain quarantine and security compliance. -  A Pilot on
boarding an inward bound vessel, shall -
(a) ascertain whether there is, or has been during the voyage, any
infectious disease on board. If there is, or has been, and the disease
is of a serious nature as laid down in the quarantine rules, he shall
anchor the vessel, hoist the quarantine signal and carry out the
instructions contained in the said quarantine rules in this respect;
and
(b) ascertain the vessel’s present draught and see that both anchors
are clear to be let go; see that the national Ensign is hoisted and the
flags denoting the name of the vessel and any other signals, as
required by Port rules from time to time, are hoisted in such a
manner as to be clearly seen from the Port signal station.

51
PART - VI
ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEDURES
37. Log Book to be kept at control (Signal) station. –  The incharge of
control station shall maintain a logbook containing such particulars as may be
specified by the Deputy Conservator, He shall also forward the logbook to the
Deputy Conservator for inspection once in a week.
38. Senior Pilots to give instructions to subordinate Pilots, Junior Pilots
and Probationary Pilots. - Harbour Master shall instruct the subordinate Pilots
to assist Junior Pilots and Probationary Pilots in all branches of a Pilot’s duty.
39. Pilots giving evidence. - A Pilot shall not attend to give evidence in any
trial or enquiry to which he is not a party, unless he is under subpoena,
without the prior permission of the Deputy Conservator and a Pilot under
subpoena to give evidence shall at once report the fact in writing to the Deputy
Conservator.
40. Pilot’s examination of charts. -  All Pilots shall attend frequently at
the office of the Deputy Conservator or Harbour Master to examine the
latest plans and charts of the port and other information concerning the
Port.
41. Pilot’s uniform. -  Pilots shall wear the prescribed uniform while on
duty and they shall abide by the normal discipline and decorum expected from
officers in uniform when dealing with their controlling officers.
42. Pilot to be provided with proper food and resting accommodation.-
The Master of a Vessel shall provide the pilot with reasonable accommodation,
if necessary breakfast, lunch and dinner, as the case may be, if the Vessel is at
anchor in the harbour and at Single Buoy Mooring (SBM) in the case of Vadinar,
failing which the Master of the respective Vessel shall pay compensation at the
rate of Rs. 200/- for any of the meals missed by the Pilot.

52
PART- VII
GENERAL
43. Interpretation. - If any question arises relating to the interpretation of
these regulations, it shall be referred to the Chairman:-
Provided that any Pilot may within sixty days of the receipt of the order
of the Chairman make a representation to the Board and the Board may make
such orders thereof as it deem fit.
44. Repeal and Savings. - On commencement of these regulations, Kandla
Port (Authorization of Pilots) Regulations 1964 stands repealed:
Provided that - (a) such repeal shall not affect the previous
operation of the said Regulations or orders or practices or anything done or
actions taken thereunder; and
(b) any proceeding under the said Regulations pending at the
commencement of these regulations shall be conducted and disposed
of, so far as may be feasible, in accordance with these regulations.

Report  
on  
The Border Roads Engineering Services Group ‘A’ (Amendment) Rules, 1988  
 
 Government of India set up the Border Roads Develo pment Board (BRDB) on 14 th  
March, 1960 to expedite road construction work in N orth East and States bordering 
neighbouring countries for socio economic developme nt of remote and far flung areas and to 
provide better road connectivity along the borders.  To execute the road projects approved by 
Government of India and included in BRDB programme,  a self sufficient departmental road 
construction work force in the name of General Rese rve Engineering Force (GREF) popularly 
known as Border Roads Organisation (BRO) was raised on 16 th  June, 1960.  
2. The Border Roads Development Board transacts its  business according to the Rules of 
Business made by the Chairman, BRDB. According to t he BRDB Rules of Business, the Board 
exercises financial and administrative powers of th e Department of Government of India, 
Ministry of Road Transport & Highways. The Financia l Advisor (Defence, Finance) is also 
financial advisor to the Board. 
3. Secretary, BRDB is an Ex officio  Joint Secretary to the Government of India, Minist ry of 
Road Transport & Highways and the Secretariat of BR DB is a department of the Ministry of 
Road Transport & Highways which is the administrati ve Ministry of GREF/BRO employees. 
GREF/BRO was made permanent department of the Centr al Government in 1969 and its 
employees were declared Central Government Civilian  employees. The service terms and 
conditions of the GREF employees are governed under  the CCA (CCS) Rules, 1965 and for 
limited purpose of discipline GREF employees are also subject to certain provisions of the Army 
Act, 1950 under Section 4(1) and 4(4) under Article  33 of the Constitution of India so that they 
can discharge their duty within strict discipline.   The fundamental right of GREF employees 
such as to form association, demonstration and stri ke against exploitation in service and 
interaction with press stand restricted as they are restricted for the Defence and Armed Forces of 
India such as Navy, Air Force, Army, CRPF ITBP, Assam Riffle, BSF etc.  
4. The Rules under examination i.e. the Border Road s Engineering Services Group ‘A’ 
(Amendment) Rules, 1988 (Annexure I ) were issued as an amendment to Schedule under  Ru le 
6 (i) of the BRES Service Rules 1977 published unde r G. S R 1554 dated 20 
th  September 1977. 

 6 
BRES Group ‘A’ (Amendment) Rules, 1988 deal with th e recruitment and appointment in the 
BRES Group “A’ Organised Central Engineering servic e and they are not merely framed for the 
recruitment but provides how the service terms and conditions of the BRES will be govern till 
the time of retirement.  
5. In context to these rules it was informed that t he Ministry of Road Transport & 
Highways undertook the amendment in the Border Road s Engineering Service Rules in 
consultation with the Department of Personnel & Tra ining, Ministry of Personnel, Public 
Grievances and Pensions and Union Public Service Co mmission along with the Ministry of Law 
in 1988. In the course of amending BRES service rul es, a provision for recruitment of Army 
officers in the equivalent grade in the Army was ma de by amending Rule 6 (i) of the BRES 
Service Rules, 1977. To facilitate recruitment of M ilitary officers in the BRES Group ‘A’ 
Central Civil Service, a provision in column No. 11  & Column No. 12 of the BRES Service 
Rules, 1988 (amendment) Schedule reading “recruitme nt of Army officers on the basis of 
posting from Army and number of posts to be filled up by the Army in each grade is to be 
decided as per the manning policy approved by the C entral Government from time to time. The 
definition of the Central Government provided in BR ES 1977 service rules reads Central 
Government means Government of India.  
6. In this background, the Committee took up for ex amination the BRES Group ‘A’ 
(Amendment) Rules 1988 and discussed in its meeting  at Gangtok, Sikkim on 4 
th  June, 2007 
with the representatives of Ministry of Defence/BRD B and Border Roads Organisation. A study 
note prepared on the meeting held at Gangtok was fo rwarded to the Ministry of Shipping Road 
Transport & Highways for their comments thereof (copy of the comments enclosed at Annexure 
II ). Some of the points raised by the Committee and the comments furnished by the Ministry are 
as follows: 
a.  The Committee enquired whether there was a compendi um of 
rules/regulations governing Border Roads Organisati on. The Secretary, BRDB stated 
that rules were framed from time to time in this re gard but no comprehensive 
legislation was in place.  
 In response the Ministry informed that there are B order Roads Regulations and 
 Record Office Instructions (ROI), which are compen dium of rules and 
 regulations governing the organisation. These are used only for references within 
 the department and cannot be quoted an authority a t par with CCS (CCA) Rules 
 and Army Act. GREF being an integral part of the A rmed Forces for the purpose 
 of Article 33 of the Constitution, Army Act/Army R ules are applicable with 
 exceptions along with other Central Service Rules.  
 

 7 
The Committee notes that 6 th  Central Pay Commission has recommended 
framing of GREF Rules despite the fact no such rule  had been framed so far. It 
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should make  all efforts to draft the 
General Reserve Engineering Force Act as soon as po ssible. The concerned 
subordinate legislation should also be framed accor dingly in the necessary time 
frame. This would clear the ambiguity regarding service rules presently imposed on 
the Civilian employees of GREF/BRO and would certai nly help to address the 
grievances of the employees. 
b.  The Committee next desired to know whether rules/re gulations framed 
concerning Border Roads Organisation had been laid on the Table of both the Houses of 
Parliament and on what date. The Secretary, BRDB was not sure about it. 
The Committee was informed that the existing rule a nd regulations are amended 
from time to time. In the past no rules/regulations  concerning BRO has been 
placed in the Parliament. Recruitment Rules of Group ‘A’ officers when amended 
will be placed in the Table of both the Houses. 
   The Committee while accepting the comments furni shed by the Ministry was 
hopeful that not only the Recruitment Rules of Grou p ‘A’ officers when amended would 
be laid before the Parliament but all Notifications  coming under the classification of 
subordinate legislation would be laid before the Pa rliament and would also be uploaded 
on the website of the Ministry for transparency and information.  
      c. The Committee noted that employees of GREF  were subject to Army Act,  1950 (as 
applicable to Army personnel/officers) but they are neither considered at par  with 
Army nor as a civilian. The pay scale sanctioned in  the 5 th  CPC has not been allowed to 
diploma engineers of BRO. Upto 4 th  Central Pay Commission, there was no 
 difference in pay scales of diploma engineers of B RO with respect to other 
similar  Central Government Department like CPWD, M ilitary Engineering 
Service and Railway.  But, in the BRO at the time o f implementation of 5 th  Pay 
Commission, diploma  engineers were put in lower sc ale, whereas officers of 
BRO and subordinates of other  categories were enjo ying the same pay scales as 
recommended by 5 th  CPC and accepted  by all Central Government depart ments. 
 In response the Ministry informed that the pay scal e of diploma Engineers BR-II, 
the 6 th  Pay Commission has recommended up-gradation and me rger of Overseer post 
with promotional post of Superintendent BR Grade-II  (present scale of Rs. 4500-7000) 
and the combined cadre extended to the scale of Rs.  5000-8000. Since the Commission 
has recommended merger of the scale of Rs.5000-8000 , Rs.5500-9000 and Rs.6500-
10500, the post will be placed in the revised pay b and PB-2 of Rs. 8700-34800 along 
with grade pay of Rs. 4200/-. Commission has also a dvised the government to implement 

 8 
this retrospectively from 1.1.96 at least for the p urpose of fixation of pay. However, 
Decision on the recommendation of 6 th  Pay Commission is to be taken by the 
Government for all employees of all Ministries/Departments.   
 d. The Committee expressed the view that members o f GREF were part and  parcel

Employment officers/staff since they were working shoulder to shoulder and  doing 
same nature of job in GREF in terms of golden principle of ‘Equal pay for equal  work’. 
  
 The Ministry on its part stated that there was no discrimination in organisation.

the opinion that resentment in the employees of an organisation was not conducive 
to its efficient functioning. Ministry should make all possible efforts to improve the 
service terms and conditions of the BRO employees s o that the working efficiency 
and morale of the employees is not adversely effected. 
  
e.      It has come to the notice of the Committee that vacancies earmarked for  GREF

 promotions whereas GREF subordinates are deprived of regular promotions.

 The Committee is of the opinion that the posting a nd appointment of Defence 
Forces personnel and officers against the civilian vacancies should not be allowed on 
adhoc  basis unless there is a provision in the Service r ules of the post that to the 
personnel posted from the Defence Forces should be eligible to hold the post i.e. 
having needed qualification and experience to  hold the post. Any personnel policy for 
appointment against civilian posts has to be catere d for the reservation provided to 
the deprived and weaker section of the society. No manning policy should be made 
without due consideration of Govt. of India particu larly deployment of Defence 

 9 
Forces officers and personnel in the civilian posts  as this may lead to serious 
consequences on the defence preparedness of the cou ntry. Therefore while making 
any policy for employment of Military trained offic ers and personnel for road 
construction work Ministry/BRDB should take into account the sparability of officers 
and personnel for civilian jobs. The Ministry/BRDB should also ensure that 
employment of Defence Forces personnel should not a ffect the promotional avenues 
of the BRO Employees.

th August, 2009

9. The Committee took up for discussion the said Ru les with the representatives from

prescribe for this. The Committee found the explana tion submitted by the Ministry of Road 
Transport & Highways/BRDB untenable and drew attent ion to its recommendation as contained 
in its 82 
nd  Report, presented to the House on 1 st  June, 1990 which states the following: 
 
 “ The Committee is unable to accept the plea of the Ministry that it is not mandatory 
upon the Administrative Ministries/Departments to l ay the rules framed under 
Article 309 of the Constitution on the Table of each House of Parliament. 
 
 The Recruitment and Conditions of Service Rules ar e made by the Government 
either under Article 309 of the Constitution or und er various Acts of Parliament. 
Whereas the Rules made under various Acts of Parlia ment are laid before 
Parliament, those made under Article 309 are not no rmally laid. The Committee 
sees no reason why the Rules made under Article 309  of the Constitution should not 
be laid before Parliament. There have been some cases where the Rules made under 
Article 309 of the Constitution have been laid befo re the Parliament. The 
Committee, therefore, strongly feels and recommends  that in order to maintain a 
uniform practice all the Rules made under Article 3 09 of the Constitution should 
also be laid before Parliament. In case, however, G overnment feels that the non-
existence of the laying provision in Article 309 is  the reason for not laying the Rules 
made thereunder, the Committee recommends that Arti cle 309 of the Constitution 
be suitably amended, so as to ensure that all the R ules made thereunder are laid 
before Parliament.” 
 [Para 4.31 of 82 
nd  Report] 
(presented on 1.6.1990) 

 11

Ministry of Road Transport & Highways/BRDB to make suitable arrangements to

 12

INTRODUCTION 
 
1. I, the Chairperson of the Committee on Subordina te Legislation, having been authorized by the 
Committee, do hereby present on its behalf, this Two Hundred and Twelfth Report of the Committee.  
2.  The Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Rajya  Sabha is constituted under Rule 204 of the Rules 
of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council  of States.  Mandate of the Committee is to scrutin ize 
and report to the Council whether the powers to make rules, regulations, bye-laws, schemes or other statutory 
instruments conferred by the Constitution or delega ted by Parliament have been properly exercised with in 
such conferment or delegation as the case may be.  The Notifications containing Rules/Regulations, etc . 
which are laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha are perused by the Committee in the light of the provisions of 
the Acts under which these were framed and also wit h a view to see whether these have been laid proper ly 
and within the prescribed form and time-frame.   
3. The Committee's concern is centered mainly aroun d the serious implications of delayed framing and 
laying of notification containing rules/regulations /orders, etc.  As part of this exercise, Committee has been 
calling the defaulting Ministries/ Departments to k now the reason for the delay, the problems faced by  them 
in laying the notifications and to find solutions to the problems.  
4. The Report has been dealt with in four parts.  T he first part deals with delay in the framing of ru les/ 
regulations under the various Acts of Parliament.  The second part deals with delay in the laying of 
Notifications on the Table of the House. The third part deals with excessive delegation of power, etc.  The 
fourth part deals with drafting of Regulations.  Th e Report on the whole contains general as well as s pecific 
observations/recommendations of the Committee on the issue.

PART I 
 
DELAY IN FRAMING OF SUBORDINATE LEGISLATION UNDER THE ACTS OF 
PARLIAMENT 
 
        The primary function of the Parliament is t o pass the legislations which become Act 
to be implemented by the government. An Act of the Parliament, in fact, creates the broad 
framework of a particular law containing an outline  of the purpose of the Act. The Parliament 
delegates its legislative authority to the executiv e to make detailed Rules/Regulations, etc. for 
administering those Acts.  These are called subordi nate legislations required to be laid before both 
Houses of Parliament after notification.  Members o f Parliament have the right to move Statutory 
Motion in the House for their modification or their  annulment altogether, if it passed by both 
Houses.   
 
2. Keeping in view the rapid growth of subordinate legislation framed under different Acts, the 
Committee took up the issue of providing a model 'L aying Formula', to be incorporated in all the 
Acts containing provision for delegation of rule-ma king powers to the Central Government. Issues 
involved in framing the said Formula were discussed  in its Fifth Report (para 20 to 25) presented to 
the House on 19 
th  August, 1968. Earlier the Committee took serious n ote of the inordinate delays in 
the framing of Subordinate Legislation and recommended the following: 
 
“ In order that such long and inordinate delays do not take place in future, the Committee 
recommends that rules and regulations required to b e made under a statute should be 
made as soon as possible but in no case later than six months from the date on which the 
statute comes into force”. 
 
[Para 48 of 9 th  Report ] 
(Presented to the House on 24.03.1971)     
 

3. The Committee pursued the implementation of the above stated recommendation and 
reported the implementation status in its subsequen t Reports.  The Committee again took up the 
issue of delay in the framing of rules/regulations when it recommended the following: 
“To avoid delays the Ministries could, to start with, frame broad but clear rules; they need 
not wait to frame all the rules on a particular sub ject in one go especially when various 
authorities/bodies have to be consulted in the matt er.  Such rules could be amended or 
new rules added subsequently on the basis of experi ence.  It is recognized that rules 
should be as perfect as possible, but this perfection should not be at the cost of expedition.  
The Ministries should also establish the practice t hat if the rules are not framed within 
this period of six months, the Secretary or the Hea d of the Department at the Secretary’s 
level should be informed accordingly , who in turn should by means of a comprehensive 
note inform the Ministries concerned and obtain his  orders thereon.  Such a note should 
invariably refer to the fact whether the particular  matter had come within the knowledge 
or comment of a Parliamentary Committee or not.  Th e Committee are persuaded to make 
this suggestion for the simple reason that for any non-compliance or excessive delay in 
compliance with the provisions of a Statute the Min ister is answerable to the House.  The 
Committee trusts that  if such a course is adopted,  the cases of such abnormal delays will 
definitely lessen”. 
[Para 56 of 10 th  Report ] 
(Presented to the House on 24.05.1971)    
4. In continuation with its commitment to ensuring that subordinate legislation framed under 
different Acts by the Ministry/Departments concerne d is brought before the Parliament and thereby 
opening it to parliamentary scrutiny by way of annu lment/modification, the Committee, after 
extensive discussions with the Ministry of Law & Ju stice, recommended the following model 
'Laying Formula' to be incorporated in all new legislations and also in the existing Acts: 
  "Every rule made by the Central Government under this Act shall be laid, as soon as 
may be after it is made, before each House of Parli ament, while it is in session, for a total 
period of thirty days which may be comprised in one  session or in two or more successive 
sessions, and if, before the expiry of the session immediately following the session or the 
successive sessions aforesaid, both Houses agree in  making any modification in the rule 
or both Houses agree that the rule should not be  m ade, the rule shall thereafter have 
effect only in such modified form or be of no effec t, as the case may be; so, however that 
any such modification or annulment shall be without  prejudice to the validity of anything 
previously done under that rule."        
[Paras 57 of the 10 th  Report] 
(Presented to the House on 24.5.1971)   
 

5. Coming to the issue under consideration the Comm ittee again took up the issue of delay in 
framing of rules/regulations and stressed the need for framing of requisite subordinate legislation 
within the given time frame and if it is not possible to do so then extension of time should be sought 
from the Committee along with the reasons for the s ame. The view of the Committee showed that 
despite the repeated attempts by the Committee the Ministries/Departments continued to delay the 
framing of rules/regulations contemplated under different Acts and also in laying them before the  
House, thereby avoiding the parliamentary scrutiny. The Committee recommended the following: 
 
‘The Committee feels that the rule making process co uld well have been completed within 
the time limit of six months which the Committee has laid down for making of rules under 
an Act after coming into force of the Act. Where ho wever, a Ministry does not find its 
possible to adhere to the time limit, they should i nform the Committee of the reasons why 
they cannot make rules within the time limit and seek extension of time for completing the 
rule making process.’ 
[Para 29 of 47 th  Report ] 
(Presented to the House on 14.09.1981)     
 
6. The Committee subsequently decided to make use o f the e-governance initiatives of the 
Government and in its 135 
th  Report took another initiative for bringing transp arency and in the 
framing of subordinate legislation under different Acts when it recommended the following: 
 
“The Committee would like to take this opportunity to recommend that Ministries, as part 
of their e-governance initiative, put all subordina te legislation on their website, preferably 
bilingually. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of Information 
Technology immediately develop a standard applicati on software with an internet 
interface for use in all Ministries, which will provide a searchable database of subordinate 
legislation linked to principal Acts administered b y the respective Ministry. Seeing the 
relative simplicity of the software the Committee h opes that this will be complete within a 
period of 6 months, and all Ministries will submit Action Taken replies in this regard 
within this period.”    
[Para 10 of 135 th  Report ] 
(Presented to the House on 27.07.2001) 

 
7. The Committee reiterated its anguish over the de lay in framing of rules/regulations and 
made the following recommendation in its 192 
nd  Report : 
 
“In addition to the concern expressed by the Committee over delay in laying of Notifications 
on the Table of the House, the Committee also expre ss its deep concern over delay in 
framing of rules/regulations under different Acts. The Committee in its 47 th  report presented 
to the House on 14.9.1981 had recommended that the rule-making process should be 
completed within a period of six months of the comi ng into force on an Act. The committee 
has further recommended that in case a Ministry is not able to adhere to this time limit, it 
should seek extension of time for completing the ru le-making process. The recommendation 
of the committee reads as follows:- 
 
 “The Committee feels that the rule-making process c ould well have been 
completed within the time limit of six months which  the Committee has laid 
down for making of rules under an Act after coming into force of that Act. 
Where however, a Ministry does not find it possible  to adhere to the time limit, 
they should inform the Committee of the reasons why  they cannot make rules 
within the time limit and seek extension of time for completing the rule-making 
process.” 
 
The Committee is constrained to take note of the fact that the Ministries/Departments 
of Government of India are not complying with the C ommittee’s recommendation to 
complete the process of framing of subordinate legi slation contemplated under various Acts 
of Parliament within a period of six months. At the  same time, the Committee also does not  
receive requests for extension of time for completi ng the rule-making process in terms of its 
recommendations as above from most of the Ministrie s/Departments. The Committee takes 
a serious note of the prevailing situation in which  the Ministries/Departments are neither 
able to complete the task of framing rules/regulati ons under different Acts within the given 
six months’ period nor do they suo-motu  approach the Committee for seeking extension of 
time. The Committee further notes that in order to ensure timely framing of rules/regulations 
it has taken an initiative to monitor the progress of framing of subordinate legislation in 
respect of all legislations brought about by differ ent Ministries/Departments of Government 
of India from the year 2003 onwards with a view to ensure that the framing of subordinate 
legislation is not delayed. The Committee, however,  finds that the responses from the 
Ministries/Departments have not been prompt in this  monitoring exercise undertaken on 
behalf of the Committee.  
  

In view of the above position, the Committee once a gain reiterates its 
recommendation that the Ministries/Departments shou ld ensure putting in place subordinate 
legislation positively within a period of six month s of the Act coming into force of the Act. 
The Committee further recommends that in case the M inistry fails to meet with this 
deadline, they should invariably approach the Commi ttee for seeking extension of time. The 
Committee further recommends that in cases where th e time limit of six months is not 
adhered to, they should, while laying rules/regulations before the Parliament invariably lay a 
statement explaining the reasons why the framing of  rules/regulations was delayed beyond 
six months so as to keep the Parliament apprised of  the compliance of the Parliament’s 
mandate  conferred upon the Executive.” 
[Para 2 ( xiv) of 192 nd  Report ] 
(Presented to the House on 24.08.2011) 
 
8. In view of the facts presented above it becomes quite evident that the Committee had been 
from its very beginning, quite concerned, about the inordinate delays in framing of rules/regulations 
contemplated under different Acts. It had in its different Reports raised the said issues alongwith the 
delay in laying of these notifications before the H ouse. It also helped resolve doubts and queries by 
way of consultations with different Ministries/Depa rtments and also by way of its 
recommendations. 
 
9. Currently at the end of each year, the Acts in w hich framing of rules/regulations are 
contemplated are identified and  followed up with t he concerned Ministries/Departments as 
regarding the position of the rules/regulations to be framed. However, despite the fact that the issue  
has been for long in the knowledge of the Committee  it is quite difficult to provide an authentic and 
reliable data regarding the Acts under which rules are to be framed and have not been framed so far. 
 
10. As part of this exercise, the Committee has bee n summoning the Secretaries of the 
defaulting Ministries/ Departments to know the reas on for the delay in framing, the problems faced 
by them in laying the notifications and to find sol utions to the problems.  The 
observations/recommendations of the Committee on th e issue of non framing of subordinate 
legislation/ delay in the laying of gazette notific ations on the Table of the House in respect of some  
Ministries/Departments have been enumerated in the succeeding paragraphs. 

 
I. Delay in the framing of subordinate legislation under the Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises Act, 2006 by the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises . 
 
11. The Committee took up the issue of non framing of rules/ regulations under the Micro, 
Small and Medium Enterprises Act, 2006 with the rep resentatives of the Ministry of Micro, Small 
and Medium Enterprises on the 19 
th  October, 2012.  The Committee took serious note of  the fact 
that framing of rules had not been completed even a fter six years of the passage of the Act.   The 
Committee observed that though the Ministry of Micr o, Small and Medium Enterprises had 
constituted the National Board for the purpose of f raming of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises 
Rules, 2006 in exercise of powers conferred to it b y Section 29 (2) (a) and (b) of the Act, it had not  
framed any rules for administration of the Fund und er Section 29(2)(c) (d) & (e) of the Act.  The 
Committee also enquired about the status of the rul es to be framed under sections 30(1) & (2) by 
State Governments.  The Ministry informed that the creation of Fund or Funds under Section 14(1) 
and (3) was an enabling provision and that Rules co uld be framed only when Government 
constituted the Fund.   However, after examination,  the Committee was of the view that 
empowering the Central Government to create a Fund was one of the aims of the Small and 
Medium Enterprises Development Bill, 2005 as mentioned in the Statement of Objects and Reasons 
of the Bill.  In response, the Secretary, Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises informed 
that the creation of a fund has to be specific to the objective of the Fund.  The fund should be a fund 
for promoting equity investment.  He clarified that  the plan outlay for the Ministry in the current 
year, i.e. 2012-13 was Rs.2,800 crores and there we re roughly 57-58 Plan Schemes. Money was 
available for development of the MSME sector throug h various Plan Schemes such as through the 
Development Commissioner, Micro, Small and Medium E nterprises (DCMSME), the Khadi & 
Village Industry Commission, the Coir Board, the Na tional Small Industries Corporation (NSIC) 
etc.   
 
12. The Ministry further informed that as far as St ate Governments are concerned, they are 
required to frame rules relating to Micro and Small  Enterprise Facilitation Councils under Sections 
21 and 30 of the Act. The Central Government has ci rculated model rules in this regard and 31 out 
of the total 35 States/UTs have so far framed rules  for setting up of the said Facilitation Councils. 

The number of States/UTs that have notified the Cou ncils stands at 34 States.  On the issue of 
framing of rules under Section 29(2) (c), (d) and ( e) of the Act, the Committee was informed that 
rules under section 29(e) has already been framed a nd a provision of 100 crores rupees has been 
made for National Innovation Fund in the Budget for year 2012-13. After approval, the rules will be 
framed and notified.  The Committee hopes that the Ministry would expedi te the framing/ 
notification of the said rules/ regulations and tak e prompt action for their laying on the Table 
of the House  at the earliest. 
  
II. Framing of rules/ regulations under the Protect ion of Plant Varieties and Farmers 
Rights Act, 2001  by the Ministry of Agriculture (Department of Agric ulture & 
Cooperation).   
 
13.   The Committee observed that the process of framing of rules/ regulations under the said Act 
had not been completed even after passing of more t han a decade. The Ministry of Agriculture 
sought extension of time on seven instances which t he Committee had no option but to grant. The 
Committee, accordingly, heard the representatives o f the Ministry of Agriculture (Department of 
Agriculture & Cooperation on the issue on 19 
th  October, 2012.  Joint Secretary, Ministry of 
Agriculture informed that the total number of rules  needed to be framed under Section 95 and 96 of 
the said Act was 67, out of which 62 have been alre ady framed by them. They were yet to frame 
remaining 5 rules. He attributed the delay in framing the rules to this being a unique Act which talks 
about farmers’ rights, plant varieties etc.  He ass ured that his Ministry would complete the task of 
framing the remaining 5 rules without any further delay.  The Committee was informed that rule for 
the establishment of Plant Protection Varieties and  Farmers’ Rights Authority (PPV&FRA) was 
notified in 2003 and it started functioning in 2005. Since then, the authority have notified guidelines 
for registration of 57 crop varieties, established 97 Desk Test Centres throughout India and set up 
the National Gene Bank for conserving different pla nt varieties.   The Chairman, PPV&FRA, 
assured the Committee that they would frame the remaining rules within six months. 
 
14. The Committee appreciates the fact that this in itially being a new subject might 
require lots of consultation while drafting the specialized rules/regulations. But a decade is too 
long a time which reflects that there was some laxi ty in this regard and lack of necessary 

importance to framing of subordinate legislation as  contemplated under the Act. The 
Committee expresses concern about the fact that alt hough the Act was passed in 2001, the 
Authority was established as late as in 2004.  Also , India being an agriculture based country 
and with important issues like introduction of Gene tically Modified (GM) Crops for field 
trials, diversion of agricultural land for non-agri cultural use, etc. cropping up lately, the 
Ministry should have expedited the framing of the r ules at the earliest. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends the Ministry to frame the r emaining rules and regulations under 
section 95 and 96 of the Act as early as possible.     
 
III  Delay in the framing of subordinate legislation by the Ministry of Environment & 
Forests.  
15.  The Committee observed that the Ministry of Environ ment & Forests were yet to finalize 
Rules on Classification, Labeling and Packaging of Hazardous Chemicals as recommended by it in 
its 99 th  Report on the Manufacture, Storage and Import of H azardous Chemicals Rules, 1989 
presented to the House on the 22 nd  March, 1993.  The Committee sought to know (i) the  reasons for 
taking so long to frame the said rules, (ii) the pr oblems/ difficulties being faced by them in the 
process; and (iii) the timeframe within which they would be able to finalize the Rules.  The 
Secretary, Ministry of Environment & Forests informed that the final Draft Rules on the subject had 
been circulated to all the Ministries and that only  final publication of the rules was pending.  The 
Ministry wanted to consult the various Ministries, i.e. Ministry of Chemicals & Fertilizers, Ministry 
of Commerce & Industry , Ministry of Agriculture, e tc., which have been vested with certain duties 
under the Rules and have specific input from them w ith respect to specific responsibilities proposed 
to be assigned to them.  Once response from the con cerned Ministries was received, the rules would 
be finalized.  The Secretary assured the Committee that entire process of finalization of the Rules 
would be completed in three months.  The Committee acknowledges the fact that lot of 
consultation goes into the drafting of specialized rules/regulations.  The Committee hopes the 
Ministry would fulfill its assurance given to it to  complete the process of finalization of the 
rules within the stipulated time-frame and their su bsequent laying before Parliament under 
intimation to it.    
 

IV Delay in the framing of subordinate legislation under the Warehousing (Development 
and Regulation) Act, 2007 by the Ministry of Consum er Affairs, Food & Public Distribution 
(Department of Food & Public Distribution)  
 
16. The Committee has been pursuing the framing of rules/ regulations under the Warehousing 
(Development and Regulation) Act, 2007 with the Min istry of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public 
Distribution (Department of Food & Public Distribution) since March 2008.  The Ministry vide their 
latest communication dated the 9 
th  July, 2013 provided a list of Rules/ Regulations framed under the 
said Act and informed that the corresponding rule t o be framed under Section 50(2) (h) was yet to 
be framed as the rule required to prescribe the min imum percentage of space to be kept reserved for 
storage of agricultural commodities in a registered  warehouse.  The number of registered 
warehouses at present was small.  After sizable num ber of warehouses were registered, thereafter 
these rules would be drafted based on experience an d difficulties faced.  Similarly, Section 51(2) 
(c), (d) & (j) provide for framing of regulations.  However, Section 9(1) to (9) provide for a brief 
procedure for disposal of goods stored in the warehouses.  Therefore, at present there appeared to be 
no need to frame regulations on this issue.  In War ehousing (Development and Regulation) 
(Registration of Warehouses Rules, 2010, provisions  had been made for the registration fee and 
security deposit for registration of warehouses.  S imilarly, in the Warehousing (Development and 
Regulation) Registration of Accreditation Agencies Rules, 2010, fee and security deposit to be 
charged from the accreditation agencies had been provided.  Therefore, there was at present no need 
to make regulations.   
 
17. The Committee observes that though the Ministry  of Consumer Affairs, Food & Public 
Distribution (Department of Food & Public Distribut ion) have framed the majority of rules/ 
regulations, a few are still in the pipeline for wa nt of time and future practical/ logistic 
requirements.  The Committee, acknowledges the fact that registration of warehouses is an on 
ongoing process, but at the same time, would like t o impresses upon the Ministry that it 
should strive to keep the delay to the minimum and take care to frame the remaining rules/ 
regulations at the first available opportunity and also ensure that the notifications are laid on 
the Table of the House without any further delay.  
 

V. Delay in the framing of the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damages Rules, 2011 and status 
of subordinate legislation contemplated to be frame d under the Civil Liability for 
Nuclear Damages Act, 2010 by the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) . 
 
18. The Secretary, DAE in a meeting held on 19 th  October, 2012 informed the Committee that 
the delay in the framing/ finalization of the rules  was due to the fact that lots of legal consultatio ns 
took place leading to the inadvertent delay.  Also,  number of documents pertaining to development 
of safety codes and safety guides is an on-going pr ocess.  It involves taking inputs from 
stakeholders which include multi-tier reviews, prio ritizing which documents need to be developed 
first and so on.  This is an on-going process.  Thu s, documents that are needed to be developed 
under the Act are under processing and would be finalized soon.   
 
19.  The Committee acknowledges the whole process of leg al consultations, development of 
safety codes and safety guides and other aspects of the matter involved in the framing of rules.  
However, the Committee feels that while the rules s hould be as perfect as possible, this 
perfection should not be at the cost of expeditious ly framing the rules.   A minimum period of 
thirty clear days from the date of the Gazette in w hich draft rules are published should be 
given to the public to send their comments thereon,  to ensure that the legal requirement of 
previous publication of the draft order is fulfilled both in letter and spirit.  In view of the time-
limit prescribed for making rules, the Ministries s hould approach the Committee for grant of 
extension of time for framing rules and the Committ ee has granted/not granted the extension 
asked for after considering all aspects of the matt er.  The Committee directs  the Department 
of Atomic Energy to complete the whole process of f raming and laying of the rules/ 
regulations under the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damages Act, 2010 at the earliest. 
 
VI Delay in the framing of Rules/Regulations under the AIIMS Act, 1956 by the Ministry 
of Health & Family Welfare (Department of Health)/ AIIMS  
  
20. The Committee has had several meetings with the  Ministry of Health & Family Welfare 
(Department of Health) and AIIMS on the issue of fr aming of rules/regulations as prescribed under 
Sections 28 and 29 of the Act. The Committee is dis mayed to know that the framing of all 

rules/regulations contemplated under the Act have n ot been done nearly 60 years after the Act has 
been passed by Parliament.  
 
21. The  Committee, in its 178 
th  Report on AIIMS Regulations, 1999 presented to the  House on 
21 st  June, 2012 pointed out that there has been gross u nder regulation under Sections 28 and 29 of 
the Act. The Committee found that the Rules/Regulat ions framed under these Sections are generic 
and lack specific details.  The Committee also foun d that the Regulations are not self-explanatory 
and at so many places matters of details are missin g and the language of the parent Act is repeated 
instead of giving elaborations. This has led to dis crepancies in interpretation and application, 
thereby causing numerous and avoidable litigations.  The Committee feels that if there is more 
clarity in the Regulations, there will be less disc retion in the interpretation and application of 
the Regulations. The Committee also feels that resp ect for administration would increase if 
procedures are followed in spirit and that this wil l prevent the faculty and employees from 
going to courts on trivial issues. In this regard, the Committee’s recommendation in its 86 th  
Report presented to the House on 07.08.1991 regardi ng use of proper and precise language 
while framing rules/regulations is reproduced here: 
 
“….. The Committee, therefore, impresses upon all c oncerned that while making rules the 
executive Ministries as also the Law Ministry shoul d ensure the use of proper and precise 
language so that not many clarification have to be issued .  In the case of the subordinate 
legislation, the intention of the makers of the rul es should be clear from the language used 
as there is no other way for the courts and others to known about it, as against in the case of 
primary legislation where it may be possible to kno wn about the intention of the framers 
from the `Statement of Objects and Reasons’ appende d to the Bills at the introduction stage 
as also from the debates in the legislatures”. 
 
 (Para 2.21 of 86 th  Report)  
    (Presented to the House on 7 th  August, 1991)  
  
22. The Committee also finds that Regulation 16 of AIIMS Regulations, 1999 is grossly 
inadequate. Regulation 16 simply states, “The Insti tute may create and appoint persons to 
Professorships, Readerships and Lecturerships and o ther posts.”  Section 29(k) of the Act has more 
clarity.  The Regulations should have more details like recruitment, promotion, seniority, 

disciplinary action, leave, etc. On whether rules/r egulations to be framed under Section 29(k) of the 
Act have been framed, notified and laid before the Rajya Sabha, the Ministry stated that this has not 
been done so far as AIIMS is an autonomous institut ion. The Committee also queried whether 
recruitment rules have been framed for posts mentio ned in Regulation 16. The Ministry replied that 
recruitment rules in respect of different categorie s of Professorship at AIIMS like Professor, 
Additional Professor, Associate Professor, Assistan t Professor, Principal of College of Nursing and 
Lecturer in Nursing are available and the same has been approved by Academic Council and 
Governing Body of the Institute. However, the Ministry stated that the same has not been notified in 
the Official Gazette as AIIMS is an autonomous institution.   
 
23. The Committee finds the argument of the Ministr y that the Recruitment Rules and 
Regulations of AIIMS need not be notified as AIIMS is an autonomous institution is fallacious, 
erroneous and very funny.  Nowhere in the Act it has been stated that AIIMS having an autonomous 
institution should not frame rules / regulations an d lay same on the Table of the House.  If 
Recruitment Rules are published and laid on the Tab le, it would not hurt the autonomy of 
institution.  The delegation has been made by Parli ament to institution to frame subordinate 
legislation to have transparency and curb arbitrari ness and discretion.  It seems AIIMS feels more 
comfortable in enjoying discretion at the expense of transparency and even violating the mandate of 
Parliament.  The AIIMS is creation of Parliament an d can not be above Parliament just by posing 
‘autonomy’, a word which has hardly been used in th e Act.  There are many statutory organizations  
in the country which have been created through   st atutory instrument and have got proper rules and 
regulations at place. Section 28 (2) of the AIIMS A ct, 1956 provides for laying of rules and Section 
29(3) of the Act provides for laying of regulations before both Houses of Parliament.  
 
24. The Committee feels that framing, notifying and lay ing of the Recruitment Rules 
would enable the Committee as well as the Members o f Parliament to get an opportunity to 
express their opinion on the said Rules and to ensu re that the Rules have been framed in 
accordance with the Act. The Committee on Subordina te Legislation, Rajya Sabha has been 
reiterating in its reports that all subordinate leg islation framed in pursuance of an Act of 
Parliament has to be laid on the Table of the House s of Parliament.  Since such 
rules/regulations come into force even before they are laid before Parliament, any delay in 

laying before Parliament, in fact, prevents Members  to exercise their right to get them 
modified/annulled by moving a Motion. In this regar d, the Committee’s recommendation in 
its 75 th  Report regarding laying of all subordinate legisla tion/orders framed in pursuance of 
powers delegated by Parliament is reproduced here: 
 
“The Committee agrees with the view of the Committee  on Subordinate Legislation, Lok 
Sabha (Seventh Lok Sabha) expressed in its 20 
th  Report that laying on the Table of all 
‘Orders’ in pursuance of powers delegated by Parliament is very significant, as it affords an 
opportunity to Members of Parliament, if they so de sire to move any amendment or 
modification to such ‘Order’, including a motion for their annulment.” 
 (Para  2.5 of 75 th  Report ) 
(Presented to the House on 29 th  March, 1988) 
 
25. The Committee is also surprised that neither In stitute nor the Ministry had compiled 
decisions taken by the Institute Body from time to time.  These decisions are important source of 
law to govern the institute.  The Institute was als o not able to provide details about decisions taken  
by joint Institute Body at Srinagar and outcome the reof.  The Institute has also created some 
standing committees.  However, regulations pertaini ng to these standing committees have still not 
been framed.  The AIIMS also operates APS (Assessme nt Promotion Scheme).  This Scheme has 
generated lots of confusion.  The Committee directs AIIMS to complete framing of regulations 
on that issue also at the earliest. 
 
26. In this respect, with regard to the Committee’s  recommendations, Ministry of Home Affairs 
has adopted a procedure which is recommended to the  rest of the Ministries also which is as 
follows:- 
“Very often delay occurs in framing of the recruitm ent rules for service/posts.  At times the 
different service/posts continue to be regulated by  draft recruitment rules or executive orders 
for a long time.  The draft recruitment rules or ex ecutive instructions are no substitute for 
statutory recruitment rules framed under proviso to  article 309 of the Constitution as unlike 
statutory rules they are not published in the gazet te and do not come to the notice of public at 
large.  The Committee are also unable to examine dr aft recruitment rules or executive 
instructions with a view to see whether any provisions therein can be so used by the executive as 

to favour or discriminate against an individual.  T he absence of statutory rules may also lead to 
discontentment among  the persons who may be or are likely to be adversel y affected as a result 
of such absence”. 
 
VII Issue of delay in the framing of subordinate le gislation under the National Institute of 
Fashion Technology Act, 2006 by the Ministry of Textiles/NIFT.  
27.  The NIFT  Act was enacted by Parliament in 2006.   Section 25  of the Act empowers the 
Board of Governors of NIFT to frame Statutes on the  subjects mentioned in Section 24, whereas 
Section 27 empowers the Senate of the Institute to frame Ordinances on the matters enumerated 
under Section 26.  Further Section 34 of the Act ma ndates that every Statute or Ordinance made 
under the Act shall be published in the Official Ga zette and laid on the Table of Both Houses of 
Parliament.  The Committee took up the status of fr aming of Statutes/ Ordinances under the NIFT 
Act, 2006 with the Ministry of Textiles in 2007. Or dinarily, the framing of subordinate legislation  
contemplated under an Act of Parliament should be c ompleted within a period of six months from 
the commencement of the Act as recommended by the C ommittee vide its 9 th  Report presented in 
1971. However, framing of Statutes/ Ordinances coul d not be completed within the six months 
period and the Ministry of Textiles had been seekin g extension of time again and again vide their 
letters dated the 29 th  November, 2007, 4 th  July, 2008, 12 th  September, 2008, 8 th  April, 2009 and 15 th  
November, 2011 . Further, the Committee enquired about (i) the rea sons for not notifying the 
Statutes and Ordinances on the subjects mentioned i n Section 24 and 26 of the NIFT Act, 2006, 
respectively and not laying them on the Table of th e both Houses, (ii) the reasons for not laying the 
Ordinance of NIFT on the Table of the House when it  was notified on 13 th  April, 2007 and sent to 
the Ministry of Textiles on 25 th  September, 2007 for laying in Parliament, and (iii ) the difficulties 
faced by NIFT in this regard.    
 
28. Thereafter, Committee decided to summon Secreta ry and DG, NIFT to explain the delay in 
framing of subordinate legislation, the Secretary, Ministry of Textiles stated that the Ministry was 
working on finalization of the Statutes from April 2007 and pending its finalization, NIFT was 
trying to systematize its procedure and establishin g standard procedures, methods and order in its 
functioning.   In 2007, the first Board of Governors met under the new Act and passed an Ordinance 
to govern the academic framework and lay down the academic  parameters.     Unfortunately,      the  

Ordinance could not be laid on the Table of the Hou se. The Statute was sent to the Law Ministry 
which raised several objections on various matters included therein.  Perhaps NIFT at that stage was 
not equipped to understand and proceed as per the Government rules.  A core Committee was set up 
to look into the matter including various other iss ues.  This procedure took a long time.  The first 
version of the draft took a year and a half and the  second took another year and a half for approval 
of the Board.  Thereafter, the Law Ministry again r aised substantive points.  This exercise had been 
completed by then.  
 
29.  The Ministry have since notified (i) The First  Ordinance of NIFT i.e. The National Institute 
of Fashion Technology for the Post Graduate Degree,  Diploma and Certificate Programme 
Ordinances, 2007, (ii) The Second Ordinance of NIFT  i.e. The National Institute of Fashion 
Technology Academic Programmes Ordinances, 2012 and  (iii) The First Statute of National 
Institute of Fashion Technology, 2012.  The Ordinan ces were laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha on 
the 2 nd  May, 2012 and the Statute was laid on 7 th  May, 2012.  Thus, the Ministry took almost five 
years to frame the ordinance and statutes to run the Institute.  The Committee does not accept 
the contention of the Ministry for the undue delay in framing subordinate legislation.  The 
Committee expressed its anguish at the attitude of the Ministry and felt that in spite of 
passage of Act in 2006, it took six years to frame the Ordinance and Statutes which are 
sketchy and hardly any matters of details.  It is o nly after the Secretary was called before the 
Committee on 19 th  October, 2012, she promised to set a time line and  complete the process 
within the stipulated schedule.   
 
30. The Committee further observed that NIFT was ye t to frame the required Statutes/ 
Ordinances to cover all the issues/ subjects as pro vided for in Sections 7, 9, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 17,  
22 and 23 so that the obligations provided for in t hese Sections are adequately fulfilled.  The 
Committee, accordingly, desired NIFT/ Ministry to f inalize the Statutes/ Ordinances and also to lay 
the same before the House within a stipulated time frame. 
 
31. The Committee observes that the Statutes and Or dinances so framed do not provide 
for the necessary details as envisaged under the Ac t. In the Committee’ s view, Parliament 

had clearly intended that delegation should be to s pecified authorities and the Statutes and 
Ordinances would be framed providing all details to  curb discretion.  However, it appears as 
if the Statute and Ordinances framed have created a  new Act.  Details are necessary so that 
these can be placed before the Committee for furthe r examination.  The Subordinate 
legislation framed under Section 24 and 26 lack det ails and appear to be in conflict with the 
parent Act.  In most of the cases where Board was s upposed to frame Statutes/ Ordinances 
with full details, same has been converted into dis cretion and further delegation has been 
provided.  The point noted was that on a number of issues like admission to various 
programmes, fees, academic input, evaluation and co nduct of examination, discipline and 
conduct, faculty development and training, intellec tual property rights, etc.,  Ordinance 15 of 
the National Institute of Fashion Technology Academ ic Programmes Ordinances, 2012 
stipulates that they should be governed by the Regu lations framed and published in the 
Academic Manuals.  This, when the Act states that t hese should be provided in the 
Ordinances.  In the Committee’s opinion, this furth er delegation for framing of Regulations 
by the Ordinance is inappropriate and is against the spirit of the Act.
